title: How to begin
hookLine: a teacher, a partner, and one line at a time
last: EAT THE FRUIT, DROP THE PEEL.

cards: A page of Talmud can look like a wall. Hebrew and Aramaic in the middle, commentaries crowding the margins, an argument already underway when you arrive, with names you don't know quoting verses you can't place.
People open it, stare at it, and close it again. The tradition has an old answer for where to start, and it isn't a book or a course. It's two people, and a very small amount of text.

teach.b: Pirkei Avot, in its first chapter, gives the advice of Yehoshua ben Perachiah: make for yourself a teacher, acquire for yourself a friend, and judge every person on the side of merit. A teacher and a friend.
Not a library. The teacher is someone a little ahead of you on the road, who can say: this word means that, this question is coming, don't panic. The friend is a partner at your level.
In study halls that partner is called a chavruta.

teach.h: TWO PEOPLE, ONE TEXT, OUT LOUD.
teach.b: Two people, one text, out loud. One reads a line and explains it; the other asks, but what about this? They argue.
The Talmud praises this kind of learning with a verse from Proverbs: "Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend."
And it warns from the other side, too: scholars who each sit alone to study, it says, grow foolish.
Then, one line at a time. A mishnah is a few sentences. A sugya, one unit of argument, can be worked through slowly with a partner, then read again the next week, clearer.
The way in isn't to master the whole thing. It's to find one person, sit across from them, and read one line slowly enough to disagree about it.
Study halls, synagogues, community classes and online programs still pair learners this way.
The form is old and simple: a teacher, a friend, a line.

how: Talmud is often studied with a chavruta, a study partner, reading aloud and debating each line, often under the guidance of a teacher in a yeshiva, synagogue class or online program.

practice: Run through the people in your life: who would read one line of something with you and argue about it kindly? Let one face come forward. Then picture the first five minutes: two chairs, one line, one question.
